constructiveParagraphs: We strongly affirm the resolution: European members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization should ratify the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.

Nuclear deterrence is a gamble with infinite stakes that requires a 100 percent success rate forever. Ratifying the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons—the TPNW—replaces Cold War brinkmanship with real security for three key reasons.

First, humanitarian risk and near misses. Deterrence relies on pure luck, not strategic genius. Lewis, 14 from Chatham House reviewed declassified documents, testimonies, and interviews and concluded the world 'has, indeed, been lucky'—with individual officers, 'often in disobedience of protocol and political guidance,' saving the day in cases like the 1983 Petrov satellite false alarm—and it flags recent warnings like the 2009 underwater collision between British and French nuclear submarines, and cases of misconduct and command-and-control laxity in the US Air Force revealed in 2013. Furthermore, Kristensen, 26 at the Federation of American Scientists estimates the US still stores about 100 B61 nuclear bombs at six airbases in five NATO countries—painting a preemptive radioactive bullseye directly on European nations. Worse, Sweeney, 20 at Defense Priorities argues these bombs are effectively useless, because the jets that would carry them cannot reliably get through Russia's air defenses in a Baltic war, while RAND's own Baltic wargames found that even modernized NATO tactical nukes would leave Russia with escalation dominance (Davis, 19).

Second, conventional superiority. Europe does not need nuclear weapons to defend itself. SIPRI, 26 figures show NATO outspends Russia over eight-to-one overall—spending 1.58 trillion dollars compared to Russia's 190 billion—and European military spending surged 14 percent in 2025, with European NATO members alone outspending Russia nearly three-to-one at 559 billion dollars. As van Hooft, 25 at RAND Europe explains, NATO's advanced fifth-generation airpower, integrated missile defense, and long-range precision strikes can raise the costs of Russian aggression by denial from the very first hours of a conflict, without ever threatening global annihilation—while European allies stay in NATO's Article 5 conventional defense as long as they give up the nuclear umbrella (Harvard Law Clinic, 18) and opt out of nuclear strategic planning, matching France's posture outside NATO's Nuclear Planning Group.

Third, financial divestment. We do not need Russia to sign the TPNW for it to work. Article 1(1)(e) of the treaty bans assisting nuclear weapons 'in any way,' which the Nuclear Weapons Ban Monitor reads to cover financing—so European ratification brings legal pressure on Europe's banks. PAX/ICAN, 23 profile 109 financial institutions already restricting nuclear weapons producers, many citing the TPNW, and institutions holding 3.9 trillion dollars named the treaty as a reason (PAX/ICAN, 22). Even more importantly, Danylyuk, 26 at the Royal United Services Institute reveals that European Union nations still paid about 781 million euros in 2025 for enriched uranium and nuclear fuel from Russia's state corporation Rosatom—whose nuclear weapons complex employed about 38 percent of its workers as of 2016, per SIPRI data. Ratifying the TPNW gives Europe a powerful legal and moral argument to cut off nearly 800 million euros a year flowing to the steward of Russia's nuclear weapons complex. We proudly affirm.

prefires.topicLabel: Does TPNW Undermine the NPT?
prefires.coreAnswer: Harvard Law's human rights clinic (Harvard Law Clinic, 19) concludes that joining the TPNW helps states better meet their NPT obligations—the TPNW does not weaken the NPT; it is exactly the kind of effective measure called for by Article VI of the NPT, which legally requires states to negotiate nuclear disarmament in good faith. You cannot undermine a treaty by carrying out its core legal requirement.

extraClauses.text: And Chatham House legal analysis (Caughley, 20) finds the claim that TPNW Article 18 lets states escape their NPT obligations does not stand up to close scrutiny—the two treaties' obligations reinforce each other.

prefires.topicLabel: TPNW Verification & IAEA Additional Protocol
prefires.coreAnswer: Hill, 21 at Chatham House notes that TPNW Article 3 adopts the NPT's own safeguards standard and goes further—legally locking in the IAEA Additional Protocol for every state that already has one, which includes every European Union NATO member through Euratom. Meanwhile, the NPT has zero verification mechanism for dismantling nuclear warheads, whereas TPNW Article 4 legally mandates verified dismantlement.

prefires.topicLabel: TPNW Article 4 'Competent International Authority'
prefires.coreAnswer: TPNW Article 4 requires states parties to designate a competent international authority to verify disarmament, and they deliberately left that choice open until a nuclear-armed state actually joins, so verification can be built around that state's real arsenal. Elimination then proceeds under a legally binding, time-bound plan negotiated with that authority and approved by the states parties.

prefires.topicLabel: Is the 1983 Petrov Incident Outdated?
prefires.coreAnswer: Lewis, 14 at Chatham House documents that nuclear near-misses did not stop in 1983—in 2009, British and French nuclear-armed submarines literally collided underwater because neither could detect the other, along with cases of misconduct and command-and-control laxity in the US Air Force revealed in 2013. Modernizing electronics only adds cyber and AI spoofing vulnerabilities to human error.

prefires.topicLabel: Why Remove US B61-12 Gravity Bombs?
prefires.coreAnswer: Sweeney, 20 at Defense Priorities shows the American B61 bombs in Europe—about 100 today (Kristensen, 26)—are effectively useless free-fall gravity bombs that require fighter jets to fly directly into Russian air defenses, and firing one needs sign-off from NATO's Nuclear Planning Group, the US President, and the host government. They only paint a nuclear first-strike bullseye on the five European countries hosting them.

prefires.topicLabel: What If Russia Uses a Tactical Nuclear Weapon?
prefires.coreAnswer: RAND's own Baltic wargames found that even modernized NATO tactical nukes would leave Russia with escalation dominance—NATO, not Moscow, would have the stronger incentive to back down (Davis, 19)—which is why RAND ranks fixing conventional forces as the top priority. NATO should deter Russian tactical nukes by threatening overwhelming conventional precision strikes against Russian forces, not by starting a mutual nuclear apocalypse.

prefires.topicLabel: Did Nukes Prevent World War III for 80 Years?
prefires.coreAnswer: Lewis, 14 at Chatham House reviewed declassified evidence and concluded the world “has, indeed, been lucky”—individual officers like Stanislav Petrov, breaking protocol during false alarms, repeatedly saved the day, not deterrence alone. Furthermore, nuclear weapons did not stop the largest conventional war in Europe since 1945 in Ukraine, nor did they stop Russian sabotage attacks across Europe from nearly tripling between 2023 and 2024, as Jones, 25 at CSIS found.

prefires.topicLabel: Russian Purchasing Power & European Munitions Gaps
prefires.coreAnswer: Even if purchasing power narrows the gap, SIPRI, 26 shows European military spending surged 14 percent in 2025—with European NATO members spending 559 billion dollars, the fastest growth since 1953, and Germany surging 24 percent to 114 billion. Furthermore, Germany alone committed about 8.3 billion euros in 2022 to 35 F-35A jets chosen to keep carrying US B61 bombs (Breaking Defense, 22)—billions that could instead fund European conventional ammunition and air defense.

prefires.topicLabel: Does Divestment Hurt Western Conventional Defense Firms?
prefires.coreAnswer: Muñoz, 26 in the Don't Bank on the Bomb report lists defense firms like BAE Systems and Leonardo among the 25 nuclear weapons producers that ethical investors shun—giving them a massive financial incentive to exit nuclear weapons work and focus on conventional European defense.

prefires.topicLabel: Russia & China State Budgets vs. Divestment
prefires.coreAnswer: Russia's state nuclear giant is still being paid by European purchases right now. Danylyuk, 26 at the Royal United Services Institute reports that European Union countries imported about 781 million euros of Russian enriched uranium and nuclear fuel in 2025 from Russia's state-owned Rosatom, whose nuclear weapons complex employed about 38 percent of its 250,000 workers according to 2016 SIPRI data. TPNW Article 1(1)(e) bans assisting nuclear weapons “in any way”—so ratifying gives European governments a powerful legal and moral argument to finish cutting off the roughly 800 million euros a year still flowing to Rosatom.

prefires.topicLabel: Why Not Sanction Rosatom Without Ratifying TPNW?
prefires.coreAnswer: Danylyuk, 26 at RUSI shows that after four years of war Russia's nuclear sector is still largely unsanctioned—Hungary and Slovakia block EU action on Rosatom—and in July 2026 Germany even approved Rosatom-licensed fuel production at the Framatome plant in Lingen. Ratifying the TPNW is each nation's own decision—no Hungarian veto—and adds a binding treaty ban under Article 1(1)(e) on assisting nuclear weapons “in any way,” giving Europe a legal and moral argument to cut off Rosatom.

prefires.topicLabel: Didn't Nuclear Weapons Financiers Rise 15%?
prefires.coreAnswer: That 15 percent jump—from 260 to 301 financiers of nuclear weapons producers (Muñoz, 26)—is the exact reason European NATO governments must ratify the TPNW now. Voluntary ESG pledges are non-binding, so some investors are already weakening their exclusions as Europe rearms; ratifying the TPNW lets governments write the treaty's ban on assisting nuclear weapons into domestic law, as Ireland already has, alongside the 109 financial institutions that already restrict nuclear producers (PAX/ICAN, 23).

prefires.topicLabel: Is the TPNW Purely Symbolic?
prefires.coreAnswer: A treaty that removes about 100 nuclear bombs from five European countries, legally binds Britain and France to verifiable disarmament, and has already been named by institutions holding 3.9 trillion dollars as a reason to exclude nuclear producers (PAX/ICAN, 22) is not symbolic—it has massive material impact.

prefires.topicLabel: Will Removing the Umbrella Cause Polish Proliferation?
prefires.coreAnswer: Poland cannot and would not build nuclear weapons: first, Poland lacks any domestic uranium enrichment centrifuge plants, plutonium reprocessing infrastructure, or even a single operational commercial nuclear reactor; second, Poland is locked into strict EU non-proliferation frameworks, compulsory Euratom fissile-material inspections, and the IAEA Additional Protocol, which TPNW Article 3 would lock in (Hill, 21), plus TPNW Article 1(1)(a) under this resolution—meaning a weapons program would breach binding EU and treaty law. In fact, Poland's own prime minister floating nuclear-related capabilities in March 2025 (Tusk, 25) suggests status quo nuclear reliance is what fuels Polish nuclear talk.

prefires.topicLabel: What About China and North Korea's Arsenals?
prefires.coreAnswer: European B61 gravity bombs have a short fighter-jet range and cannot reach China or North Korea, while the US strategic nuclear triad of missiles, submarines, and bombers—not Europe's B61s—covers the Indo-Pacific. In fact, van Hooft, 25 at RAND notes the United States prioritizes the Indo-Pacific, leaving Europe to shoulder more of its own deterrence against Russia.

prefires.topicLabel: What About Russian Tactical Nukes in Belarus?
prefires.coreAnswer: When Vladimir Putin announced tactical nuclear weapons for Belarus in March 2023, he said “the United States has been doing this for decades”—pointing straight at US bombs in NATO Europe as his precedent (Al Jazeera, 23). Ending NATO nuclear sharing strips Moscow of that diplomatic excuse for forward-deploying tactical warheads.

prefires.topicLabel: Will the US Pull Troops Out of Europe?
prefires.coreAnswer: The United States stations conventional troops in allied nations that refuse nuclear weapons on their soil in peacetime, including Norway, Denmark, and Spain. Sweeney, 20 at Defense Priorities explains that the B61 bombs serve no purpose except to escalate a local crisis in the Baltics into a potential strategic calamity—so removing them keeps a European border incident from dragging America into nuclear war.

prefires.topicLabel: Won't Russia Target European Bases Anyway?
prefires.coreAnswer: Hosting about 100 B61 bombs at Büchel, Kleine Brogel, Volkel, Aviano, Ghedi, and Incirlik (Kristensen, 26 at FAS) turns six airbases in five countries into obvious first targets for Moscow. Removing nuclear weapons removes the incentive for a preemptive nuclear strike.

prefires.topicLabel: Does Nuclear Sharing Deter Terrorism or Iran?
prefires.coreAnswer: You cannot deter a decentralized terrorist network by threatening to drop a B61 nuclear gravity bomb on a city, and storing about 100 nuclear bombs across six European airbases (Kristensen, 26) only creates high-value targets for terrorist sabotage or theft—Kristensen, 08 at FAS exposed a US Air Force review finding most European nuclear weapon sites needed significant additional resources to meet Pentagon security requirements.

prefires.topicLabel: Is the Disarmament Transition Period Dangerous?
prefires.coreAnswer: Under TPNW Article 4, nuclear-armed states do not disarm overnight; they take warheads off alert immediately, then eliminate them under a legally binding, internationally verified plan within ten years—extendable by up to five—while NATO's military, backed by 1.58 trillion dollars in spending (SIPRI, 26), and the US strategic arsenal remain fully operational throughout the entire transition.

prefires.topicLabel: Will Conventional Defense Cost Europe More Money?
prefires.coreAnswer: Nuclear weapons do not save money—ICAN, 26 documents that the nine nuclear-armed states spent a record 118.8 billion dollars on nuclear weapons in 2025, up 19 percent in a single year, and Germany alone committed about 8.3 billion euros to 35 F-35A jets chosen to keep carrying US B61 bombs (Breaking Defense, 22)—billions locked into a nuclear mission instead of usable conventional defense.

prefires.topicLabel: Why Not Just Upgrade Cyber & Radar Systems?
prefires.coreAnswer: Lewis, 14 at Chatham House finds the probability of inadvertent nuclear use is not zero and is higher than had been widely considered—in the 1995 Norwegian rocket scare, Boris Yeltsin opened Russia's nuclear briefcase with only minutes to decide before crews confirmed it was a harmless science rocket. The only way to guarantee zero accidental detonation in Europe is removing the warheads.

prefires.topicLabel: Didn't Deterrence Stop Direct NATO-Russia War Over Ukraine?
prefires.coreAnswer: Williams, 24 at CSIS shows Russia used nuclear threats as part of its strategy to deter direct Western intervention in Ukraine—while NATO's B61 bombs did not deter Russia's invasion. Even with nuclear weapons in Europe, Russia launched the largest European invasion since World War II and nearly tripled sabotage attacks across Europe from 2023 to 2024 (Jones, 25).

prefires.topicLabel: Why Haven't Any NATO Members Ratified Yet?
prefires.coreAnswer: YouGov polling for ICAN found 77 to 89 percent support for joining the TPNW in Belgium, Denmark, Iceland, Italy, the Netherlands, and Spain (ICAN, 21), two former NATO Secretaries-General—Javier Solana and Willy Claes—signed a 2020 letter urging allies to join (ICAN, 20), and Washington has openly pressured countries to drop the treaty (AP, 20), which is why the resolution asks what European NATO members should do.

prefires.topicLabel: Didn't Finland and Sweden Join NATO for the Nuclear Umbrella?
prefires.coreAnswer: Finland and Sweden joined NATO after Russia invaded Ukraine, and Sweden—following the longstanding Norwegian and Danish model—still keeps a peacetime policy against nuclear weapons on its territory while remaining a full NATO ally (Defense News, 26).

prefires.topicLabel: Won't France & the UK Lose Their UN Security Council Seat?
prefires.coreAnswer: Article 23 of the United Nations Charter names France and the United Kingdom as permanent Security Council members by country name, with zero mention of possessing nuclear weapons. Ratifying the TPNW does not affect their UN veto power in any way.

prefires.topicLabel: Why Remove US B61 Bombs From Incirlik in Türkiye?
prefires.coreAnswer: Kristensen, 26 at FAS estimates the US still keeps 20 to 30 B61 nuclear gravity bombs at Incirlik Air Base in Türkiye, and storing them there—where Türkiye was expelled from the F-35A stealth fighter program after buying Russian S-400 air defenses and sits minutes from Middle East conflict zones—is a massive security liability that offers zero deterrence value.

prefires.topicLabel: What If Russia Threatens Europe After Ratification (Article 17)?
prefires.coreAnswer: TPNW Article 17 explicitly allows any state party to withdraw from the treaty, with twelve months' notice, if extraordinary events related to the treaty's subject matter jeopardize its supreme national interests, while NATO's military, backed by 1.58 trillion dollars in spending (SIPRI, 26), and the US strategic triad remain intact every single day.

prefires.topicLabel: How Does Europe Counter Russian Nuclear Missiles in Kaliningrad?
prefires.coreAnswer: Slow B61 free-fall gravity bombs that need sign-off from NATO's Nuclear Planning Group, the US President, and the host government cannot intercept or deter fast Iskander missiles in Kaliningrad. As van Hooft, 25 at RAND explains, conventional tools—integrated air and missile defense and long-range precision strike—can raise the costs of Russian aggression from the very first hours of a conflict.

prefires.topicLabel: Don't Nuclear Weapons Deter Russian Chemical or Biological Attacks?
prefires.coreAnswer: The Biological Weapons Convention of 1972 and Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993 banned those weapons globally without NATO needing to threaten chemical or nuclear retaliation against civilians, and NATO's overwhelming conventional superiority deters chemical escalation without violating humanitarian law.

prefires.topicLabel: Don't Steadfast Noon Nuclear Exercises Signal Alliance Resolve?
prefires.coreAnswer: Kristensen, 22 at FAS notes NATO ran its Steadfast Noon nuclear-strike drill in October 2022 in the middle of the largest conventional war in Europe since World War II, timed almost alongside Russia's own strategic nuclear exercise—exactly the mirror-image signaling that feeds escalation, whereas conventional NATO exercises demonstrate credible battlefield defense without rehearsing nuclear war.

prefires.topicLabel: With New START Expired in 2026, Isn't Disarming Dangerous?
prefires.coreAnswer: The collapse of bilateral arms control like New START is the exact reason Europe must strengthen multilateral disarmament norms through the TPNW and cut off the roughly 781 million euros a year Europe pays Rosatom, a key steward of Russia's warhead complex (Danylyuk, 26), rather than fueling an unconstrained arms race.

prefires.topicLabel: Won't Dismantling UK & French Arsenals Destroy Defense Jobs?
prefires.coreAnswer: Under TPNW Article 4, verified warhead dismantlement and submarine conversion can take up to 15 years of high-skilled engineering work, and SIPRI, 26 shows European military spending surged 14 percent in 2025—with European NATO members spending 559 billion dollars— creating massive demand for conventional naval and aerospace workers.

prefires.topicLabel: Doesn't the Guided B61-12 on Stealth F-35A Jets Fix the B61's Flaws?
prefires.coreAnswer: Putting a guided tail-kit on a B61-12 bomb mounted on a short-range F-35A still requires sign-off from NATO's Nuclear Planning Group, the US President, and the host government, and RAND's Baltic wargames found even modernized NATO tactical nukes would leave Russia with escalation dominance (Davis, 19). Upgrading the bomb only makes nuclear escalation more tempting.

prefires.topicLabel: If Every Other Country Has Nukes, Why Not Europe?
prefires.coreAnswer: 184 out of 193 United Nations member states do not have nuclear weapons—including 23 European NATO allies right now with zero nuclear weapons on their soil—because hosting nuclear weapons paints a first-strike target on your soil rather than protecting you. Europe does not need nuclear weapons when NATO outspends Russia more than eight-to-one overall at 1.58 trillion dollars, as SIPRI, 26 confirms, and the United States still deploys roughly 1,700 strategic warheads outside Europe (Kristensen, 26).

prefires.topicLabel: Wouldn't Europe Have No Defense / Be Defenseless Without Nukes?
prefires.coreAnswer: Europe is never defenseless without nuclear weapons: SIPRI, 26 shows NATO outspends Russia more than eight-to-one overall—spending 1.58 trillion dollars compared to Russia's 190 billion—and European NATO members alone outspend Russia nearly three-to-one at 559 billion dollars. As van Hooft, 25 at RAND Europe explains, conventional tools—long-range precision strike, fifth-generation airpower, and integrated air and missile defense—can raise the costs of Russian aggression from the very first hours of a conflict, without threatening global suicide.

prefires.topicLabel: Why Should Europe Disarm First Before Russia Does?
prefires.coreAnswer: Waiting for Vladimir Putin to disarm first means keeping nuclear targets on European soil forever. constructiveParagraphs: We strongly negate the resolution: European members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization should ratify the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.

Unilaterally disarming European democracies does not make nuclear-armed autocracies lay down their weapons. As the North Atlantic Council, 20 officially warned, a world where the states that challenge the international rules-based order have nuclear weapons, but NATO does not, is not a safer world. Stripping away Europe's nuclear deterrent creates a catastrophic power vacuum, for three key reasons.

First, the TPNW hands Russia a 100 percent European nuclear monopoly and invites nuclear blackmail. The Pro side tries to shrink this resolution to forward-deployed B61 gravity bombs, yet the resolution binds all European NATO members—which under TPNW Articles 1 and 4 legally forces Britain and France to destroy all 515 of their sovereign nuclear warheads, most on continuous-at-sea missile submarines (van Hooft, 25), and strips every ratifying ally of the US nuclear umbrella—as even Harvard Law's pro-ban clinic concludes (Harvard Law Clinic, 18). Meanwhile, Kristensen, 26 at FAS estimates that Russia retains about 4,400 warheads, including about 1,800 tactical nuclear warheads built for battlefield use. prefires.topicLabel: When Is It Acceptable to Incinerate Millions of Civilians?

prefires.topicLabel: If Russia Uses a Tactical Nuke, Do We Fire One Back?

SOURCE_CARDS.title: Too Close for Comfort: Cases of Near Nuclear Use and Options for Policy
SOURCE_CARDS.citation: Dr. Patricia Lewis, Dr. Heather Williams, Benoît Pelopidas, and Sasan Aghlani, Chatham House Report, April 28, 2014 (Updated May 18, 2023).
SOURCE_CARDS.takeaway: 13 cases of near nuclear use (1962–2002), including the 1983 Petrov false alarm, plus recent incidents (the 2009 UK/French submarine collision and 2013 US Air Force misconduct) that raise concern about safety and command-and-control laxity, show the world has been lucky—with individuals, often in disobedience of protocol and political guidance, saving the day on several occasions.
SOURCE_CARDS.verbatim: “Evidence from many declassified documents, testimonies and interviews suggests that the world has, indeed, been lucky, given the number of instances in which nuclear weapons were nearly used inadvertently as a result of miscalculation or error… individual decision-making, often in disobedience of protocol and political guidance, has on several occasions saved the day.” The report also points to the 2009 collision of French and UK submarines and to US Air Force misconduct revealed in 2013 as cause for concern about current safety, security, and command and control.

The main contributor to the global increase in military spending in 2025 was a 14 per cent rise in Europe to $864 billion... The 29 European NATO members spent a combined total of $559 billion in 2025...
